text: Data leakage is the most expensive mistake in applied machine learning, because it doesn't crash anything. Your code runs, your validation score is superb, and the model then collapses in production. Leakage means information that wouldn't be available at prediction time has sneaked into training or evaluation, so the score describes a model that cheats.

First kind: target leakage. A feature leaks the target when it's a consequence of the outcome, recorded after the thing you're predicting. Predicting churn with a refund_issued column — refunds are typically issued when a customer cancels, so the column carries the answer, but at prediction time, the customer hasn't cancelled yet and there's no refund to look at.

Simulating churn that depends on tenure and support tickets, then adding that leaky refund column: a model trained on honest features alone gets 72.2 percent test accuracy, comfortably beating the 58.2 percent majority-class baseline. Add the refund column, and accuracy leaps to 96.3 percent — on a proper held-out test set.

Nothing in the split protected us, because the leak is inside the features themselves. A model deployed on live customers, who have no refund yet, would fall straight back toward the honest 72 percent, or worse. The test for target leakage: for every feature, ask, will I actually know this value at the moment I need to make the prediction?

Second kind: train-test contamination. This happens when information from the test rows influences training through preprocessing. Anything that learns from data — choosing features, computing means for scaling, filling missing values — must be fitted on the training set only, then applied to the test set.

Here's a striking demonstration using pure random noise — labels nobody could genuinely predict. Picking the 20 best of 1,000 noise features once before the split, the wrong way, versus once after the split, the right way, across 30 runs.

Selecting features before the split scores 78.7 percent on labels that are literally coin flips — the test labels leaked into which columns were kept. Done properly, selecting after the split, it scores 51 percent, which is exactly chance. The same trap applies to scaling — computing the mean and standard deviation on the whole dataset before splitting lets test statistics leak into training.

The fix is always the same order of operations: split first, then fit every transformation on the training rows only, then apply it to validation and test rows. Other forms to watch for: temporal leakage, where random splits on time series let the model train on the future; duplicate rows appearing in both train and test; and leaky identifiers that happen to correlate with the outcome.

Warning signs: a score far better than similar published work or common sense, a single feature that dominates everything, or performance that drops sharply after deployment. When a model looks too good, assume leakage until you've proved otherwise. To recap: prevent target leakage by asking whether each feature is known at prediction time, and prevent contamination by splitting first and fitting every transformation on training data only.
